content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose an automaton based method for skill transfer from a source to a target environment. The assumption is that source and target environments are different MDPs, but their reward functions share a certain structure which can be captured (approximately) by an automaton.

Compared to previous methods, there are two key novelties:
1.) Instead of solving the 'abstract' MDP created by the automaton and then using the resulting Q-values to guide learning in the target environment, the authors propose to solve the source environment (or assume an oracle there) and distill those Q-values into the 'abstract' MDP, which is then used to guide the learner in the source environment. They claim that this produces Q-values in the abstract MDP that are more suitable for the target environment if the abstract MDP is misspecified in some way (e.g. by not capturing the temporal extension of actions).
2.) The authors propose a new way to distill the abstract Q-values into the target domain. Instead of modifying the rewards using potentials (like previous work) they let the abstract Q-values influence the DQN 'target' Q-value in the target domain -- and anneal their influence over time. This allows the correct solution to be recovered even if the abstract Q-values are wrong.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

The premise that a known reward structure, for example in the form of an automaton, can be used to guide the learning process is interesting -- I agree that suitable prior knowledge is available in many situations.
Furthermore, the two novelites (which I outlined above) seem genuinely novel and address important limitations of previous methods.


## Weaknesses

My two main concerns regard the presentation and experiment section. I will discuss both in turn below.

### Presentation

I found the presentation of the paper a bit confusing and I felt a bit like a detective trying to figure out what was novel and why it was relevant. The information was mostly there, but, in my opinion, could be arranged better. For example, the extensive discussion of CRM and problems under $\gamma <1$ is crucial to understanding the motivation of the paper and should be taken out of the related work section (which I personally often skip on first reading). 

As a second point, why was the definition of the labelling function changed from $L: S\times A\times S \to \Sigma$ in Icarte (2022) to $L: S \to \Sigma$? This is not discussed at all -- and I'm also not sure it makes sense. For exmple, in the experiments, how can $L$ map to a predicate like 'wood' or 'sword' (which corresponds to *picking up* the object) if it only knows the current state of the inventory and not its *change*?

I think the Preliminaries section could be improved by, for example, mentioning the *purpose* of DFAs (accepting or rejecting a string -- which is not clear from context). Furthermore, a better discussion of where the proposed method would fail would also help the reader put this method into context.

### Experiments

It looks to me as if the experiments are on a single random seed. If this is the case, this is insufficient -- especially on such environments. 
In my experience, for these types of "exploration heavy environment" where the agent either finds the solution or doesn't, the point in time when the reward jumps from "unsolved" to "solved" is quite random and to get a good estimate a lot of repetitions are required. I wouldn't feel confident about any result under 30 repetitions.

It would also be great to show the Q-values that were learned or distilled into the abstract MDPs -- this would greatly help in understanding the method and supporting the claims made about why static/dynamic transfer is better than e.g. CRM.

Lastly, I couldn't find any hyperparameters used. Apologies if I missed them.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As discussed, the work is novel, but the presentation could be improved, hyperparameter seem to be missing and the experimental support is currently insufficient.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The authors propose an interesting idea, but, in its current form, I believe the paper is not yet ready for publication. 
Improvements to the structure of the paper could greatly help the reader undrestand it better, in particular its relation to previous work and how previous shortcomings are addressed.
Furthermore, the experiments require more repetitions. Additional information on the results (for example showing and discussing the abstract distilled Q-values), would further improve the section.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes to address sample efficiency in Deep RL by representing RL objectives from a source domain (teacher environment) in a high-level symbolic representation in terms of a finite-state automata and using this to initialize q-values of an agent in a new environment (student environment). Q-values of the teacher environment are estimated from experience and are encoded into the corresponding automaton by pairing the original state of the environment with a corresponding state in the automaton. The automaton then acts as a bridge to transfer q-values between the source and target environments. The goal is to initialize q-values of target environment such that the agents learns to achieve higher rewards with less exploration. The paper proposes two approaches for knowledge transfer, static and dynamic, in which in the former value iteration (or q-learning) over an abstract representation is used to estimate initial q-values and in the latter q-values are estimated from a teacher environment.

The proposed method is evaluated on 3 grid-world environments, in which the experimental setup is to the 7x7 versions as the teacher environment and the corresponding 10x10 version as student environments. The two transfer approaches were compared against a published static transfer baseline and standard DQN without transfer, and they were shown to outperform both. In particular, dynamic transfer demonstrated superior performance in terms sample efficiency.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

The paper demonstrates that incorporating high-level symbolic knowledge into a low-level learning problem helps to address sample efficiency. Furthermore, it shows that estimating that symbolic knowledge from experience in a similar environment captures the environment dynamics better and results in better task performance. This was demonstrated on different benchmark tasks.

Weaknesses

The approach assumes that the objectives between the source and target domains are identical, which limits its general application. 
The approach is only evaluated on grid-world environments in which it's relatively easy to construct corresponding automata. Even then, the differences between the source and target environments are grid sizes. How much of a challenge does this constitute? 
Also, it's not clear if the approach can generalize to even bigger grid sizes. Why stop at 10x10?
It seems unfair to compare to a baseline DQN that has no prior knowledge given that the transfer approach are provided prior knowledge in terms q-value estimates from the teacher environment. It would be more fair if the DQN baseline was also trained in a teacher environment and then fine-tuned on the student environment without any knowledge distillation. Also, time taken to estimate initial q-values should be considered when comparing sample efficiency.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written, easy to follow and is of good quality. The paper should be easy to reproduce with an understanding of finite-state automata and the automated compilers. The idea of converting RL objectives into symbolic representations is not novel however the paper proposes extracting objectives from experiences in related domains, which doesn't seem to be considered in related approaches.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper makes many assumptions that affect its general application. Also, it's only demonstrated on simple grid-world environments with small differences between source and target environments. It's not clear if this can be considered a general knowledge transfer framework for real-world reinforcement learning problems. Also, the baseline approach [1] was evaluated on more benchmarks including continuous control tasks, whereas this paper only evaluates on simple discrete environments. Thus, it's not clear if this paper is really advancing the state of the art.

[1]. Icarte, R. T.; Klassen, T. Q.; Valenzano, R.; and McIlraith, S. A. 2022. Reward machines: Exploiting
reward function structure in reinforcement learning. Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research
73:173–208.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on the issues of sample inefficiency and poor generalization on tasks outside the training distribution for deep learning based methods. To address the issues, a neuro-symbolic transfer learning based on automaton distillation is proposed by distilling Q-value estimates from a teacher into a low-dimensional representation in the form of an automaton. Specifically, two strategies of generating Q-value estimates are proposed, such as static transfer and dynamic transfer. Finally, experiments were conducted on three types of grid-world environments, including Blind Craftsman, Dungeon Quest, and Diamond Mine, with results demonstrating its effectiveness in terms of performance and sample efficiency.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Neuro-symbolic methods have shown promising in improving the generalization capability and sample efficiency in deep reinforcement learning (RL). This work targets to resolve the issues of sample inefficiency and poor generalization by utilizing linear temporal logic within the teacher-student paradigm, which would be interesting to both communities of knowledge representation and RL.


Weaknesses:
- The presentation of the paper should be improved. For example, what's the difference between the source task (teacher) and target task (student)? what are the differences in nodes and transitions when mapping states and actions in the source and target domains? how does value estimates interact with automaton transitions? what's the specific knowledge that would be transferred beween teacher and student? It's said in the paper that this knowledge is the information about the reward signal, is it represented by the Q-values in a tabular form?
- In Figure 1, the automaton is defined based on the "rewards" where each one corresponds to an entire history of observation instead of just the rewarding state, is that true? If this is the case, are there some overlapped states in different observation histories? How are those nodes in the automaton beneficial for the RL?
- For the static transfer, are the Q-value estimates generated from the automaton for the source domain? For the dynamic transfer, what's this pre-trained DQN? Is it trained in the source domain? How to map teacher Q-values of state-action pairs to the transition in the automaton? Is this automaton for the source or target? 
- what's the labeling function in practice?
- distill knowledge from a teacher automaton to a student DQN: do the Q-values in both the teacher task and student task keep the same tabular form? or what's the difference between those two representations w.r.t. Q-values?
- The organization of the paper is somewhat hard to follow. It looks the content for the sections of preliminary and related work is mixed together. The caption is missing for the figure on pp.5.
- The literature review is suggested to discuss different ways of constructing the low-dimensional abstraction of the original state space by using symbolic representation, such as the work of [1,2,3].
- The current empirical evaluation is weak. Firstly, the domains are not challenging enough to demonstrate the needs of transfer learning between source and target domains. Secondly, each of these tasks, such as Blind Craftsman, Dungeon Quest, and Diamond Mine, has a hierarchical structure which is more suitable for the hierarchical methods. Therefore, it's unfair to compare the proposed methods with a vanilla Q-learning. It should include some of hierarchical methods as the baselines. Lastly, there lacks the ablation study for the proposed methods. Therefore, the current empirical results could not well support the claims on sample efficiency and generalization ability.



References:
- [1] Konidaris, G., Kaelbling, L., & Lozano-Perez, T. (2014, June). Constructing symbolic representations for high-level planning. In Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (Vol. 28, No. 1).
- [2] Illanes, L., Yan, X., Icarte, R. T., & McIlraith, S. A. (2019). Leveraging Symbolic Planning Models in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning. In KR2ML Workshop at NeurIPS.
- [3] Yang, F., Lyu, D., Liu, B., & Gustafson, S. (2018, July). PEORL: integrating symbolic planning and hierarchical reinforcement learning for robust decision-making. In Proceedings of the 27th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (pp. 4860-4866).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- This paper could be improved by re-organizing and presenting more details of the problem setting & proposed method as I mentioned in the main Weaknesses. Besides, there are some questions that could be clarified.
- It's somewhat novel in the methodology, although it's based on the previous work of linear temporal logic for automaton and the teacher-student paradigm for knowledge distillation.
content.summary_of_the_review: According to my comments in both the main Weaknesses and the section of Clarity, Quality, Novelty, I feel this is a paper where reasons to reject outweigh reasons to accept.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents two transfer methods to generate Q-value estimates. The failure modes of the existing methods are analyzed and better policies are presented.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths:

1. Applying neural-symbolic techniques in RL is very important and I appreciate the novelty and significance of the proposed ideas.
2. The proposed approach is supported by the theory and the theory looks correct.
3. The proposed environment looks interesting and is a good testbed for neural symbolic approaches.

# Weaknesses

1. The proposed methods are not motivated well. Why distillation is used in RL? Why two domains are involved? Why is the proposed method called neural-symbolic? What's the relationship with the previous literature, such as program-guided agents, or programmatic RL approaches? Moreover, why don't the authors use PPO instead of vanilla DQN?

2. The environments seem to be too small. Why don't the authors conduct environments on other neural-symbolic RL literature (for example, following programmatic RL or ComPILE or other literature)? 

3. The writing is poor. For example, the figures are raw and are not very informative. Figure 4 looks blurry.

4. No quantitive results are presented in this paper. So it is hard to evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The overall quality is poor. And the proposed algorithms might have significant flaws.
content.summary_of_the_review: No significant results are presented. Writing is raw. The methods are not very sound.

content.title: Automaton Distillation: A Neuro-Symbolic Transfer Learning Approach for Deep RL
content.TL;DR: Transfer reinforcement learning using symbolic knowledge extracted from a teacher
content.abstract: Reinforcement learning is a powerful tool for finding optimal policies in sequential decision processes. However, deep learning methods suffer from two weaknesses: collecting the amount of agent experience required for practical RL problems is prohibitively expensive, and the learned policies exhibit poor generalization on tasks outside the training distribution. To mitigate these issues, we introduce automaton distillation, a form of neuro-symbolic transfer learning in which Q-value estimates from a teacher are distilled into a low-dimensional representation in the form of an automaton. We then propose two methods for generating Q-value estimates: static transfer, which reasons over an abstract MDP constructed based on prior knowledge, and dynamic transfer, where symbolic information is extracted from a DQN teacher. The resulting Q-value estimates from either method are used to bootstrap learning in the target environment via a modified DQN loss function. We list several failure modes of existing automaton-based transfer methods and demonstrate that both static and dynamic automaton distillation decrease the time required to find optimal policies for various decision tasks.
